Rising Blood Sugar in Young Adults Hurts Midlife Brain Health

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A 30-year longitudinal study reveals that young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually rises over decades face significantly worse cognitive health by midlife, even if they never develop Type 2 diabetes.
  • While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.
  • Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A 30-year longitudinal study reveals that young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually rises over decades face significantly worse cognitive health by midlife, even if they never develop Type 2 diabetes. Tracking nearly 3,000 adults from age 18 into their mid-50s, researchers found lower memory, processing speed, and executive function scores among those with rising glucose trajectories, alongside structural brain changes in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes.

Source: American Heart Association.

While Type 2 diabetes has long been recognized as a risk factor for late-life dementia, cognitive impairment linked to blood sugar was historically thought to emerge primarily after age 65.

Now, a three-decade investigation published today in the Journal of the American Heart Association demonstrates that creeping elevations in fasting blood sugar starting in young adulthood can measurably undermine memory, processing speed, and executive function by middle age, even among individuals who never cross the diagnostic threshold into full-blown diabetes.

Led by first author Dr. Regina Paradela (postdoctoral researcher at the University of São Paulo Medical School and neuroepidemiologist at the Global Brain Health Institute at UC San Francisco) and senior author Dr. Kristine Yaffe (director of the Center for Population Brain Health at UC San Francisco), the study tracked metabolic and cognitive trajectories across 2,808 participants in the landmark Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults (CARDIA) cohort.

Industry observers note that enrolled between 1985 and 1986 at ages 18 to 30 across four U.S. cities, participants underwent repeated fasting blood glucose measurements over 30 years until reaching an average age of 55. At the 30-year mark, all participants completed comprehensive neuropsychological testing, and a subset of 605 participants underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

By mapping longitudinal glucose patterns across the 2,463 participants who remained free of Type 2 diabetes, the researchers identified three distinct metabolic trajectories:.

An additional 345 participants developed Type 2 diabetes (fasting glucose ≥126 mg/dL) during the 30-year follow-up.

Even after adjusting for demographic and lifestyle factors, both the increasing-glucose group and the Type 2 diabetes group performed significantly worse on tests of memory, processing speed, executive function, and global cognition compared with the lower-stable glucose group.

“The fact that increasing glucose levels were associated with poorer cognitive performance, even among people who had not developed Type 2 diabetes during the 30-year study, is very important,” explained Paradela. “This suggests that changes in glucose metabolism may be relevant to brain health earlier in adulthood than we typically think about.”.

Furthermore, MRI scans revealed tangible anatomical footprints among participants who developed Type 2 diabetes, who exhibited less total gray matter and more abnormal white matter tissue, markers closely tied to accelerated brain aging and cognitive decline.

“Future research should evaluate whether monitoring and managing increasing glucose levels earlier in adulthood can prevent or delay cognitive decline and structural brain changes,” noted senior author Yaffe.

Commenting on the study, Dr. Elisabeth Marsh, professor of neurology at The Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine and chair of the writing group for the American Heart Association’s 2026 scientific statement Brain Health Across the Life Span, emphasized the value of early vascular and metabolic care: “The American Heart Association’s Life’s Essential 8 offers steps to improve heart and brain health and support cognitive well-being at every stage of life.”.

Can rising blood sugar harm brain health even if you don’t have diabetes?

Yes. Over a 30-year study, young adults whose fasting blood sugar gradually increased into the prediabetic range (110–115 mg/dL) scored significantly worse on midlife tests of memory, processing speed, and executive function than peers whose blood sugar remained low and stable, even though they never developed Type 2 diabetes.

What structural brain changes were seen in participants who developed Type 2 diabetes?

MRI brain scans revealed that adults who developed Type 2 diabetes by their mid-50s had less total gray matter volume and more abnormal white matter tissue compared to those who maintained lower-stable blood sugar levels from young adulthood.

When should adults start paying attention to blood sugar for brain protection?

Industry observers note that researchers note that changes in glucose metabolism begin affecting cognitive performance much earlier than age 65. Monitoring and managing blood sugar trajectories starting in young adulthood, using healthy nutrition, physical activity, and cardiovascular risk control, may help protect midlife and late-life brain health.

Funding: Co-authors, disclosures and funding sources are listed in the manuscript.

Trajectories of Fasting Blood Glucose and Brain Health in Middle Age.

Recent findings suggest that research on associations between long‐term fasting blood glucose (FBG) trajectories and brain health in early adulthood is limited. We investigated associations of FBG trajectories with cognition and brain structure.

In a recent development, participants were from the CARDIA (Coronary Artery Risk Development in Young Adults) study, followed for 30 years, who completed ≥1 cognitive test at year 30. Among participants without diabetes with ≥3 FBG measurements from baseline to year 30, we identified FBG trajectories using latent growth mixture models. Participants who developed diabetes after baseline were included for comparison (n=345). Cognition was assessed using tests of processing speed, executive function, memory, fluency, and global cognition. Structural magnetic resonance imaging data from 605 participants included total gray matter volume and white matter lesions. Associations were examined using multivariable linear regression adjusted for demographics and health behaviors.

We included 2808 participants (mean age, 55.2±3.6 years; 56% women; 44% Black individuals). Three FBG trajectories were identified: lower‐stable (n=1387), moderate‐stable (n=938), and increasing (n=138). Compared with the lower‐stable group, increasing FBG and incident diabetes were associated with worse performance in memory, processing speed, executive function, and composite cognition; increasing FBG was also associated with worse global cognition. Incident diabetes was associated with lower total and parietal gray matter volume and greater parietal white matter abnormalities. No consistent sex or race interactions were observed.

Persistently elevated glucose below the diabetes threshold was associated with worse cognitive performance in midlife, while incident diabetes was associated with structural brain changes.

Why Nerve Pain Lingers

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (906 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury.
  • Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.
  • It has been revealed that for millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers uncovered a molecular pathway in the spinal cord that drives persistent neuropathic pain long after an initial nerve injury. The multi-omics and electrophysiological study reveals that nerve injury suppresses the nuclear regulatory protein Nono, triggering a steep drop in Kcnq2 potassium channels that normally calm spinal pain neurons, while restoring Nono reverses pain hypersensitivity in animal models.

Source: Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine.

It has been revealed that for millions of people living with neuropathic pain, even a feather-light touch or a mild shift in temperature can ignite excruciating discomfort long after an initial physical injury has healed. Rather than stemming solely from ongoing tissue damage at the original wound site, persistent nerve pain is frequently driven by central sensitization, a state in which pain-processing circuits inside the spinal cord become hyperexcitable and amplify ordinary sensory signals.

Now, a comprehensive study published in Research by scientists at Guizhou University of Traditional Chinese Medicine, Fudan University, and partner institutions has pinpointed a critical molecular switch behind this spinal hyperexcitability: the Nono–Kcnq2 regulatory axis.

By combining five layers of molecular profiling with single-neuron electrophysiology and behavioral testing, the team demonstrated how nerve injury silences a vital genetic brake inside spinal neurons—and demonstrated that restoring this pathway alleviates chronic pain sensitivity.

In a recent development, under healthy conditions, neurons in the spinal cord’s dorsal horn rely on specialized potassium channels to stabilize their electrical charge and prevent runaway firing. When potassium ions flow out of a neuron, they keep excitability in check; when those channels disappear, neurons fire rapidly in response to minimal stimulation.

To trace why potassium channel control breaks down after nerve trauma, the investigators examined a rat model of chronic sciatic nerve constriction, which produces pronounced mechanical and thermal pain sensitivity within three days. Electrophysiological recordings confirmed that spinal dorsal horn neurons fired far more readily while exhibiting sharply diminished outward potassium currents.

Applying an integrated multi-omics pipeline, spanning proteomics, phosphoproteomics, transcription factor profiling, spatial transcriptomics, and single-cell RNA sequencing across 48,279 spinal cord cells, the researchers mapped the exact cellular shifts occurring at seven and 21 days post-injury:.

According to recent reports, molecular binding experiments confirmed that Nono directly binds to a conserved region of the Kcnq2 gene promoter to drive its expression. To test whether repairing this broken link could relieve pain, the researchers delivered an adenoviral vector carrying Nono into the spinal region of nerve-injured rats.

According to recent reports, increasing Nono expression successfully rebuilt Kcnq2 protein abundance, restored protective outward potassium currents in dorsal horn neurons, and significantly eased mechanical and thermal pain hypersensitivity. When the team applied XE991, a selective pharmacological blocker of Kcnq2/3 potassium channels, both the restored potassium currents and the behavioral pain relief were largely reversed, confirming that Nono alleviates pain specifically by reactivating Kcnq2 channels.

While the researchers emphasize that clinical therapies remain a long-term goal—noting that experiments were conducted in male rats and that additional pathways also contribute to neuropathic pain—the findings illuminate a clear mechanistic bridge linking gene transcription to electrical excitability in the spinal cord.

Rather than merely masking pain signals with broad analgesics, future therapies aimed at preserving Nono activity or supporting Kcnq2 potassium channel function could help quiet overactive spinal circuits at their molecular source.

Why can neuropathic pain persist even after a nerve injury has healed?

Following nerve trauma, neurons in the spinal cord can undergo central sensitization, becoming abnormally excitable so that they amplify harmless signals like light touch or mild warmth into intense pain.

What did researchers discover about the Nono and Kcnq2 proteins in the spinal cord?

In a recent development, scientists found that nerve injury reduces the activity of the nuclear protein Nono, which normally switches on the Kcnq2 gene. Kcnq2 produces potassium channels that act like electrical brakes to calm spinal neurons; when Kcnq2 levels drop by up to 80%, pain neurons fire excessively.

Did restoring Nono reduce pain sensitivity in the animal study?

Yes. When researchers used a viral vector to restore Nono expression in the spinal cord of rats with nerve injuries, Kcnq2 potassium channel levels rebounded, neuronal firing calmed down, and the animals showed significantly less sensitivity to mechanical and thermal pain.

Multi-Omics Analysis Reveals Nono–Kcnq2 Regulation of Neuronal Excitability in Chronic Constriction Injury-Induced Neuropathic Pain.

In a recent development, neuropathic pain, resulting from somatosensory nervous system damage or disease, is a debilitating condition marked by spontaneous pain, hypersensitivity, and sensory abnormalities. Neuropathic pain involves spinal neuronal hyperexcitability, yet its molecular basis remains poorly defined.

We utilized a comprehensive multi-omics approach, incorporating proteomics, phosphoproteomics, concatenated tandem array of consensus transcription response elements, and both single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, to chart time-resolved adaptations in the L4 to L6 spinal cord of a chronic constriction injury rat model.

In a recent development, multi-omics revealed remodeling of glutamatergic synapse pathways and identified non-POU (Pit-Oct-Unc) domain-containing octamer binding (Nono) as a down-regulated transcription factor associated with reduced potassium voltage-gated channel subfamily Q member 2 (Kcnq2) expression. Nono and Kcnq2 were co-enriched in neurexin 3-positive and peripherin-positive spinal neurons.

Restoring Nono expression up-regulated Kcnq2, enhanced K+ outward currents (an effect largely abolished by the Kcnq2/3 blocker XE991), and alleviated pain hypersensitivity. Mechanistically, Nono was enriched at a conserved Kcnq2 promoter region in vivo and enhanced Kcnq2 promoter activity in reporter assays.

Together, these findings established a Nono–Kcnq2 transcriptional axis that constrained spinal excitability and suggested a therapeutic entry point for neuropathic pain.

Breaking: Mysterious brain activity under anesthesia challenges what we know about consciousness

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1410 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness.
  • "Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," mentioned Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even when a person is fully unconscious under general anesthesia, their brain may still be doing something remarkable: processing language, recognizing patterns, and even anticipating which words will come next.

Sources indicate that researchers at Baylor College of Medicine have discovered that the brain retains surprisingly sophisticated abilities during anesthesia, despite the absence of conscious awareness. The findings, published in the journal Nature, challenge traditional assumptions about the relationship between consciousness and thinking. They could also provide new insights into how the brain processes memories and language, potentially leading to advances in technologies that help people communicate after neurological injuries.

"Our findings show that the brain is far more active and capable during unconsciousness than previously thought," mentioned Dr. Sameer Sheth, professor and Cullen Foundation Endowed chair of neurosurgery and a McNair Scholar at Baylor. "Even when patients are fully anesthetized, their brains continue to analyze the world around them.".

Recording Brain Activity During General Anesthesia.

In a recent development, to investigate what happens inside the unconscious brain, Sheth, who is also a neurosurgeon at Baylor St. Luke's Medical Center, and his colleagues studied patients undergoing epilepsy surgery while under general anesthesia.

In a recent development, these procedures offered an unusual opportunity to examine the hippocampus, a brain structure deeply involved in learning and memory. Located within the brain's temporal lobe, the hippocampus helps organize information and plays an important role in forming newly introduced memories.

The researchers used advanced recording devices called Neuropixels probes to monitor electrical signals from hundreds of individual neurons in the hippocampus. These tiny probes can detect activity from many nerve cells simultaneously, providing a detailed picture of how groups of neurons respond to information.

Industry observers note that according to the researchers, this technology had not previously been used to investigate this particular brain region in this way. It allowed the team to examine how the hippocampus responds to sounds and language while patients are unconscious and unable to report what they experience.

The first experiment involved playing a series of repeating tones, occasionally interrupted by a sound that differed from the others.

Although the patients were under anesthesia, neurons in their hippocampus responded differently to the unexpected sounds. Even more surprisingly, the brain cells became better at distinguishing these unusual tones as the experiment continued.

This improvement suggested that the hippocampus was showing signs of neural plasticity, the brain's ability to change its responses through experience. In other words, some of the basic processes associated with learning appeared to remain active even without conscious awareness.

The Unconscious Brain Can Process Language and Predict Words.

The researchers then tested whether the unconscious brain could handle something more complicated than simple sounds.

They played short stories to the anesthetized patients while continuing to record activity from neurons in the hippocampus.

In a recent development, the results revealed a surprising level of language processing. Distinct patterns of neural activity contained information about different categories of words, including nouns, verbs, and adjectives. This suggested that the hippocampus was responding to meaningful features of language rather than simply detecting that sounds were occurring.

But the most intriguing discovery went a step further.

In a recent development, the researchers found that neural activity also carried information that could be used to predict upcoming words in a sentence. Even though the patients were unconscious, their brains appeared to anticipate how the language unfolding around them might continue.

"The brain appears to anticipate what comes next in a story, even without conscious awareness," said Sheth, who is also Director of The Gordon and Mary Cain Pediatric Neurology Research Foundation Laboratories within the Duncan Neurological Research Institute at Texas Children's Hospital.

Industry observers note that this ability is related to a process known as predictive coding. Rather than passively receiving information, the brain continually uses patterns and previous experience to anticipate what might happen next. When listening to someone speak, for example, the brain can use the words already heard to form expectations about what is likely to follow.

In a recent development, scientists have typically studied this kind of sophisticated prediction in people who are awake and paying attention. Finding evidence of it during general anesthesia suggests that at least some of the underlying neural processes can operate independently of conscious awareness.

"This kind of predictive coding is something we associate with being awake and attentive, yet it's happening here in an unconscious state," stated Dr. Benjamin Hayden, professor of neurosurgery at Baylor.

What Does This Discovery Mean for Consciousness?

The findings raise important questions about what consciousness actually contributes to the brain's ability to process information.

Industry observers note that consciousness is generally associated with subjective awareness, including the experience of hearing, thinking, and understanding the world around us. Yet the study suggests that some neural processes involved in interpreting language and predicting future information can continue even when that awareness is absent.

Recent findings suggest that this does not necessarily mean that the anesthetized patients consciously understood the stories being played to them. Instead, it indicates that the brain can carry out surprisingly complex aspects of language processing without a person being aware of doing so.

The distinction could help researchers better understand how consciousness emerges.

One possibility is that awareness depends not simply on whether individual brain regions remain active, but on how information is coordinated and shared across larger networks of brain regions.

Under this view, a structure such as the hippocampus might continue analyzing information even when the broader communication between brain regions needed for conscious experience is disrupted.

A Surprising Connection Between the Brain and Artificial Intelligence.

The discovery also highlights an intriguing similarity between human brain activity and artificial intelligence (AI).

Large language models, the technology behind many modern AI chatbots, generate text by using patterns learned from enormous amounts of language data to predict what should come next.

The researchers observed a related predictive ability in the hippocampus, where neural signals reflected information about upcoming words even during unconsciousness.

Although biological brains and AI models operate in fundamentally different ways, both can use patterns in language to anticipate future information. Studying these similarities may help scientists better understand how prediction works in natural and artificial systems.

The findings could also have practical implications for brain-computer interfaces, which use signals recorded from the brain to communicate with external devices.

One potential application involves speech prosthetics, technologies designed to help people communicate when injuries or neurological conditions have impaired their ability to speak.

If scientists can reliably identify meaningful language signals in the brain, those signals might eventually be used to support communication technologies for patients who have lost speech abilities.

"Can we use these signals to deploy and run a speech prosthetic for some of the parts of the brain that are damaged by stroke or injury? These are questions that we can now consider in relation to this part of the brain," said Dr. Vigi Katlowitz, first author and a neurosurgery resident with Baylor.

Scientists Are Rethinking the Limits of the Unconscious Brain.

Despite the striking results, the researchers emphasize that several questions remain unanswered.

The experiments were conducted under one particular type of general anesthesia, so the findings cannot automatically be extended to other anesthetic methods or states of unconsciousness.

It is also unclear whether similar language processing occurs during sleep or coma, two conditions that differ significantly from medically induced unconsciousness.

It has been revealed that another important limitation is that the researchers focused on the hippocampus. Further studies will be needed to determine whether comparable abilities persist in other brain regions and how these areas interact when consciousness is absent.

Nevertheless, the results provide compelling evidence that unconsciousness does not necessarily mean the brain has stopped performing sophisticated information processing.

Instead, the brain may continue analyzing patterns, responding to unexpected events, and anticipating language even when a person has no conscious awareness of the surrounding world.

"This work pushes us to rethink what it means to be conscious," remarked Sheth. "The brain is doing much more behind the scenes than we fully understand.".

Some pieces set the colored letters on white, while others flood the ground with a single saturated color and let the type push back. The folded program carries the full stack in a run of blue, green, yellow, orange, red, and purple, with the small sans serif keeping the facts straight at the top of the sheet.

Industry observers note that the caps are the most tactile piece of the set, the lettering stitched small across white, green, and pale blue cotton. An orange sign stands on the tiled floor, and the word SALOON stretches across a wood doorway in the same blocky letters, proof the alphabet holds its shape from a poster down to a doorway. Pentagram has designed identities for Storefront since 2012, and this one plays the longest with the room it was made for.

Breaking: Adolescent Brain Circuits Shape Lifelong Social Drive

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (800 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that fresh research reveals that adolescence is a critical developmental window for a brain pathway linking the prefrontal cortex to the ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR).
  • Industry observers note that adolescence is widely recognized as a period of intense behavioral and social transformation, marked by heightened peer seeking, shifting relationships, and emotional turbulence.
  • Now, new findings from The Ohio State University Department of Psychology pinpoint a critical developmental window inside a pathway linking the brain’s executive command center to its reward hub: the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that fresh research reveals that adolescence is a critical developmental window for a brain pathway linking the prefrontal cortex to the ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR). The study highlights that temporarily quieting this reward-and-motivation circuit during adolescence leads to lasting social withdrawal in adulthood, shedding light on why psychiatric conditions like depression and schizophrenia often emerge during the teenage years.

Source: The Ohio State University.

Industry observers note that adolescence is widely recognized as a period of intense behavioral and social transformation, marked by heightened peer seeking, shifting relationships, and emotional turbulence. While neuroscientists have mapped early infant brain development in granular detail, the exact neural mechanisms sculpting social behavior during the teenage years remain far less understood.

Now, new findings from The Ohio State University Department of Psychology pinpoint a critical developmental window inside a pathway linking the brain’s executive command center to its reward hub: the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit.

Industry observers note that presented at Neuroscience 2026, the annual meeting of the Society for Neuroscience, by lead author and doctoral candidate Katrina Lin alongside senior investigator Dr. Laurence Coutellier, the study demonstrates that disrupting PFC-vSTR maturation during adolescence permanently dampens adult social motivation.

To establish how social drive naturally evolves across the lifespan, Lin and Coutellier first measured spontaneous social investigation in both adolescent and adult mice, whose compressed three-week adolescent window enables researchers to trace developmental trajectories across adulthood.

In a recent development, “I always say it’s like two dogs in a park. They start sniffing each other. They’re careful at first, and then they go into a different type of sniffing behavior,” explained Coutellier, associate professor of behavioral neuroscience at Ohio State. As predicted, adolescent mice exhibited substantially higher motivation to initiate social interaction than adult mice.

“In humans it’s the same,” Coutellier noted. “A teenager loves to hang out with their friends, and they will seek this interaction. As adults, we will be more careful. We don’t approach a stranger just like that, and we’ll be more cautious about the way we interact. There’s still a strong social motivation, which is necessary for us to have social relationships, but there is less of it.”.

The prefrontal cortex, which governs decision-making, impulse control, and social reasoning, and does not finish maturing in humans until roughly age 25, sends direct signals to the ventral striatum, a core hub for reward processing and motivation.

To test whether adolescent maturation of this pathway is essential for adult sociability, the team selectively switched off activity in PFC-vSTR neurons in both male and female mice during either adolescence or adulthood:.

“We found that actually, yes, if we prevent the maturation of the frontal circuit to the striatum, when mice reach adulthood they have impaired social motivation,” Coutellier said.

Understanding how the PFC-vSTR pathway wires itself during adolescence carries significant implications for psychiatry. Conditions such as depression and schizophrenia frequently manifest during the teenage years, often preceded or accompanied by profound social withdrawal.

Next, Coutellier’s laboratory intends to examine how real-world environmental stressors, such as prolonged adolescent social isolation, alter the maturation of this circuit.

Industry observers note that “We can try to study what happens when our mice don’t get to socialize, and we can think about what happened during COVID-19, when teenagers were told to stay home and stop socializing to be safe. How did that impact this developmental trajectory of the social circuits?” Coutellier asked. “We’re trying to understand what genetic and environmental factors can make these symptoms arise at the time of adolescence — not before, and not in adulthood, but during that sensitive period of development.”.

What is the PFC-vSTR brain circuit, and what does it do?

According to recent reports, the prefrontal cortex–ventral striatum (PFC-vSTR) circuit connects the prefrontal cortex (the brain’s decision-making and social control center) to the ventral striatum (a key hub for reward and motivation). During adolescence, this pathway matures to support healthy social motivation and peer interaction.

Why did turning off this pathway in teenage mice affect them as adults, while adult mice bounced back?

Recent findings suggest that researchers found that adolescence is a uniquely sensitive developmental window when this circuit is still actively wiring itself. Disrupting it during adolescence permanently altered how the circuit matured, leading to reduced social motivation in adulthood, whereas adult brains already have established wiring that recovered immediately once the inhibition ended.

How does this research relate to mental health conditions like depression and schizophrenia?

Industry observers note that many psychiatric disorders first appear during the teenage years and involve social withdrawal. Identifying the exact brain circuits that mature during adolescence helps scientists understand how genetic risks or environmental stressors, such as social isolation, can derail healthy social development.

Funding: This research was supported by a Whitehall Foundation Grant.

#138802. Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain

📅 17 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1523 w)

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Scientists discover how deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat, and boosts the brain

📅 17 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1523 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed.
  • It has been revealed that scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production.
  • It has been revealed that now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A good night's sleep does much more than leave you feeling refreshed. During deep sleep, the body releases growth hormone, a powerful chemical messenger that helps build muscle, strengthen bones, and regulate fat metabolism. For teenagers, getting enough sleep is especially vital because growth hormone plays a major role in reaching their full height potential.

It has been revealed that scientists have long known that insufficient sleep can interfere with growth hormone production. What remained unclear was exactly how the brain controls this process, particularly during non-REM sleep, the deep, restorative stage that typically dominates the earlier part of the night.

It has been revealed that now, researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, have uncovered the brain circuitry behind this relationship. In a study published in the journal Cell, the team identified the neurons that regulate growth hormone release during sleep and discovered a previously unknown feedback system that helps maintain a delicate balance between hormone levels and wakefulness.

The discovery reveals that the relationship works in both directions. Sleep stimulates growth hormone production, but growth hormone also sends signals back to the brain that influence when we wake up.

The findings could eventually help scientists develop new approaches to treating sleep disorders associated with metabolic diseases such as diabetes, as well as neurological conditions including Parkinson's and Alzheimer's.

In a recent development, "People know that growth hormone release is tightly related to sleep, but only through drawing blood and checking growth hormone levels during sleep," said study first author Xinlu Ding, a postdoctoral fellow in UC Berkeley's Department of Neuroscience and the Helen Wills Neuroscience Institute. "We're actually directly recording neural activity in mice to see what's going on. We are providing a basic circuit to work on in the future to develop different treatments.".

Why Deep Sleep Matters for Growth and Metabolism.

It has been revealed that growth hormone is best known for its role in childhood development, but its importance extends well into adulthood. It supports the maintenance of muscle and bone, helps the body regulate how it uses stored fat, and influences blood sugar levels.

When sleep is consistently disrupted, growth hormone regulation can suffer. Because this hormone helps control glucose and fat metabolism, inadequate sleep may contribute to an increased risk of obesity, diabetes, and cardiovascular disease.

Industry observers note that to understand how the brain coordinates these processes, the Berkeley researchers focused on a region called the hypothalamus. Located deep within the brain, this small but essential control center helps regulate hunger, body temperature, hormone production, and the daily cycle of sleeping and waking. Its basic functions have been preserved throughout mammalian evolution.

Within the hypothalamus, the researchers examined neurons that produce growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and two distinct types of neurons that produce somatostatin.

These chemical messengers have opposing functions. GHRH encourages growth hormone secretion, while somatostatin suppresses it. Together, they help control how much growth hormone enters the bloodstream, largely by regulating its release from the pituitary gland, a small hormone-producing structure at the base of the brain.

The scientists also investigated how growth hormone influences the locus coeruleus, a region in the brainstem involved in alertness, attention, thinking, and the drive to explore newly introduced or unfamiliar experiences.

Disruptions in the activity of this region have been linked to several psychiatric and neurological disorders.

Recent findings suggest that "Understanding the neural circuit for growth hormone release could eventually point toward new hormonal therapies to improve sleep quality or restore normal growth hormone balance," stated Daniel Silverman, a UC Berkeley postdoctoral fellow and study co-author. "There are some experimental gene therapies where you target a specific cell type. This circuit could be a novel handle to try to dial back the excitability of the locus coeruleus, which hasn't been talked about before.".

Scientists Map the Brain Circuit That Controls Growth Hormone.

The research was conducted in the laboratory of Yang Dan, a professor of neuroscience and of molecular and cell biology at UC Berkeley.

It has been revealed that to investigate how the circuitry works, the team studied mice using electrodes implanted in their brains. The scientists recorded neural activity while using light to stimulate specific neurons in the hypothalamus, allowing them to observe how different parts of the system responded.

In a recent development, mice are particularly useful for studying sleep regulation because their sleep patterns differ significantly from those of humans. Rather than sleeping through one long stretch each night, mice typically sleep in brief episodes lasting only several minutes, scattered throughout the day and night.

This gave the researchers repeated opportunities to examine how neural activity and growth hormone regulation changed as the animals moved between sleeping and waking.

Using advanced techniques to trace connections between brain cells, the team discovered that GHRH and somatostatin behave differently depending on the stage of sleep.

Recent findings suggest that during rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, the stage commonly associated with vivid dreaming, activity involving both GHRH and somatostatin increases. Although these hormones normally exert opposing effects, their coordinated activity during this stage contributes to increased growth hormone release.

During non-REM sleep, the pattern changes. Somatostatin activity decreases, reducing its inhibitory influence, while GHRH activity rises moderately. This combination also promotes growth hormone secretion.

The discovery helps explain how different sleep stages can support the release of the same essential hormone through distinct patterns of brain activity.

Growth Hormone Also Helps Control When We Wake Up.

Perhaps the most surprising finding was that growth hormone does not simply respond to signals from the sleeping brain. It also influences the brain circuits that control wakefulness.

As growth hormone gradually builds up during sleep, it stimulates neurons in the locus coeruleus, increasing their activity and helping promote the transition toward waking.

This creates a feedback loop in which sleep encourages growth hormone release, and the resulting hormone activity helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Sources indicate that the researchers also identified an unexpected complication. Although greater activity in the locus coeruleus generally promotes alertness, excessive stimulation can have the opposite effect.

In an earlier study published the same year, Silverman demonstrated that when neurons in this region become overexcited, they can paradoxically promote sleepiness rather than wakefulness.

Together, these findings reveal a carefully regulated system in which the brain must balance competing signals to maintain healthy sleep and hormone activity.

Scientists describe this type of self-regulating process as homeostasis, the body's ability to maintain stable internal conditions even as its environment and physiological demands change.

"This suggests that sleep and growth hormone form a tightly balanced system: Too little sleep reduces growth hormone release, and too much growth hormone can in turn push the brain toward wakefulness," Silverman said. "Sleep drives growth hormone release, and growth hormone feeds back to regulate wakefulness, and this balance is essential for growth, repair and metabolic health.".

A Surprising Connection Between Sleep and Brain Health.

The newly identified feedback system may have implications that extend beyond physical growth and metabolism.

Because the locus coeruleus helps regulate attention, alertness, and cognitive function, growth hormone's influence on this region suggests it could also play a role in how effectively the brain functions after waking.

This raises the possibility that maintaining healthy sleep and growth hormone rhythms may support both physical recovery and mental performance.

"Growth hormone not only helps you build your muscle and bones and reduce your fat tissue, but may also have cognitive benefits, promoting your overall arousal level when you wake up," Ding mentioned.

By identifying the specific brain cells and signaling pathways involved, the researchers have provided a foundation for exploring therapies that target disrupted sleep and hormone regulation.

Recent findings suggest that such approaches could eventually prove useful for people with sleep disturbances related to metabolic disorders or neurological diseases. However, the experiments were conducted in mice, and additional research will be needed to determine how these mechanisms operate in humans and whether they can be safely targeted with treatments.

According to recent reports, the findings underscore a fundamental principle of sleep biology: Rest is not simply a period when the brain switches off. It is an active, carefully coordinated process in which hormones and neural circuits constantly communicate to support growth, repair, metabolism, and wakefulness.

Research Funding and Contributors.

The research was supported by the Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI), which supported Dan as an HHMI investigator until the year of the study's publication, and the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair fund.

Dan holds the Pivotal Life Sciences Chancellor's Chair in Neuroscience.

Additional co-authors include Peng Zhong, Bing Li, Chenyan Ma, Lihui Lu, Grace Jiang, Zhe Zhang, Xiaolin Huang, Xun Tu, and Zhiyu Melissa Tian of UC Berkeley, along with Fuu-Jiun Hwang and Jun Ding of Stanford University.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • New neuroimaging research reveals that the human brain uses a distinct predictive strategy when listening to spoken Mandarin compared to Indo-European languages.
  • To keep pace with the rapid flow of natural conversation, the human brain does not simply wait passively for words to arrive.
  • Until now, however, most neurobiological models of predictive speech processing have been built almost exclusively on studies of English and other Indo-European languages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New neuroimaging research reveals that the human brain uses a distinct predictive strategy when listening to spoken Mandarin compared to Indo-European languages. The study indicates that while Mandarin listeners simultaneously track phonemes, sub-syllables, characters, and words, predictive brain signals occur primarily at the sub-syllabic level, where lexical tone integrates with speech sounds, rather than at the level of individual phonemes.

To keep pace with the rapid flow of natural conversation, the human brain does not simply wait passively for words to arrive. Instead, auditory and language circuits continuously forecast upcoming sounds, syllables, and words, generating neural “surprise” signals whenever spoken input deviates from expectation.

Until now, however, most neurobiological models of predictive speech processing have been built almost exclusively on studies of English and other Indo-European languages. How the brain anticipates speech in tonal, logographic-linked languages such as Mandarin Chinese, where pitch contours alter word meaning and syllables serve as tightly unified building blocks, has remained far less explored.

In a study published in eNeuro, researcher Qifei Wang and colleagues at Radboud University investigated how the unique structural and tonal architecture of Mandarin shapes real-time neural predictions during naturalistic listening.

To capture the brain in action during continuous speech comprehension, the research team recorded neural activity from 34 native Mandarin speakers as they listened to an audiobook.

By modeling the acoustic and linguistic properties of the story alongside the participants’ brain responses, the investigators discovered that neural activity simultaneously tracked multiple nested units of spoken Mandarin:.

Next, the team analyzed how strongly the brain anticipated incoming speech at each linguistic level by measuring neural responses to expected versus surprising sounds.

In a striking departure from prior findings in Indo-European languages, the researchers detected no clear evidence of predictive neural signaling at the individual phoneme level in Mandarin. Instead, predictive effects stood out most strongly at the sub-syllabic level, where lexical tone contributed significantly when integrated with other speech-sound features.

This divergence highlights how the brain adapts its computational strategy to match the structural rules of a speaker’s language: whereas Indo-European listeners rely heavily on fine-grained phoneme transitions to forecast words, Mandarin listeners anchor their predictions to larger, tone-integrated sub-syllabic units.

By demonstrating that understanding Mandarin relies on parallel, multi-level linguistic predictions centered on tone-integrated sub-syllables rather than isolated phonemes, the study underscores the importance of linguistic diversity in cognitive neuroscience, showing that universal models of human language must account for how different writing and tonal systems organize speech inside the brain.

How does the brain keep up with fast spoken conversation?

Industry observers note that rather than passively waiting to hear every sound, the brain actively predicts upcoming speech elements based on context. When incoming speech is surprising or unexpected, the brain generates distinct neural responses that help upgrade comprehension in real time.

How does processing spoken Mandarin differ from English and European languages?

Industry observers note that in English and other Indo-European languages, the brain strongly predicts speech at the level of individual sounds (phonemes). In Mandarin, Radboud University researchers found no clear predictive effects at the phoneme level; instead, the brain makes its strongest predictions at the sub-syllabic level, where pitch tone combines with speech sounds.

What units of speech did the brain track while listening to a Mandarin audiobook?

Brain recordings from 34 native Mandarin speakers demonstrated that the brain simultaneously tracks four nested layers of spoken Mandarin at once: individual phonemes, sub-syllables, characters, and full words.

Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing During Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.

According to recent reports, language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation.

Here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations.

According to recent reports, we recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels.

In contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components.

These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties.

Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages.

Using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level.

These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, which has been closed for two years for renovations, will reopen on 1 December. Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, confirmed that the museum, which was initially scheduled to reopen in January, will now open at the beginning of next month with several newly introduced galleries, according to a post on an official government Facebook page last week. The ministry and the museum's director Luma Yas Jasim al-Douri had not replied to a request for comment at the time of publication.

Several notable artefacts and specially curated wings have been prepared for public display, according to the newspaper Iraqi News, which obtained an official document about the reopening from the ministry. These include Assyrian statues and reliefs comprising monumental winged bulls (lamassu), stone carvings depicting Assyrian kings and cuneiform collections. The newly introduced Abbasid and Islamic galleries will display intricately carved wooden mihrabs and monumental calligraphic friezes, as well as mosaics and stone relics.

The reopening of Iraq’s national museum—which houses tens of thousands of Mesopotamian, Sumerian, Babylonian and Assyrian antiquities and was closed for various periods after it was looted in 2003 during the US-led invasion—is a priority for Al-Dakhili who was sworn in last month as part of the newly introduced government under Ali al-Zaidi. In an official statement on 25 October, Al-Dakhili mentioned the museum's importance and added that there are prepares afoot for “a new building that befits the historical and civilisational value of Iraq”.

Paul Collins, the keeper of the Middle East Department at the British Museum who has worked with Iraqi colleagues to develop partnerships in support of museums and heritage in the country, tells The Art Newspaper that the reopening of the Iraq Museum “is an key moment, reflecting Iraq’s strong commitment to preserving its world-renowned cultural heritage and promoting heritage tourism”.

Industry observers note that according to another Facebook post from the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities—formerly known as the Ministry of Culture, Tourism and Antiquities until the tourism portfolio was separated from it in October as part of government restructuring under Al-Zaidi—tourism is seen as a way to attract foreign investment. Recently, dozens of foreign delegations have visited Ur, the site of the Sumerian ziggurat and the birthplace of the Prophet Abraham, located within the Dhi Qar governorate and Nasiriyah where Al Dhakili is from.

A number of museums have opened in Iraq in recent months while upcoming ones been announced. On 15 November, the Abbasid Palace in Baghdad reopened to the public in an official ceremony, according to Iraqi News. Last month, Iraq’s first Jewish museum opened in Baghdad in the restored Shamash Jewish School, which was founded in 1928. The museum displays personal objects, photographs and documents from Iraq’s once prominent Jewish community and pays tribute to prominent Jewish Iraqi figures such as the vocalist Salima Murad and Sassoon Heskel, who served as the modern state of Iraq’s first finance minister.

Ali Al-Dakhili, Iraq's Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, has announced that a upcoming museum will open in the former Presidential Palace in Babylon Photo: Hadani Ditmars.

Meanwhile, according to a spokesperson for the World Monuments Fund, the long-awaited reopening of the Mosul Museum, looted in the aftermath of the 2003 invasion and ransacked by ISIS in 2015, will take place next spring.

Al-Dakhili has also declared that the openings of three new museums in Nineveh, Diyala and Diwaniyah governorates are imminent and that “logistical procedures are ongoing to complete the opening of a museum in Babil Governorate within the Presidential Palace” (the former ruler Saddam Hussein’s old palace located within the site of Babylon). The museum will feature “archaeological and heritage collections for the governorate, highlighting its status in the history of human civilisation”, the statement claims.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

According to recent reports, validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you initiative to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

Forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as promptly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

In a recent development, side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

Recent findings suggest that one of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Manufacturer). Here is the honest comparison.

Industry observers note that A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

In a recent development, self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

According to recent reports, deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

According to recent reports, the biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

It has been revealed that the 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

Batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice says to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

According to recent reports, but here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

It has been revealed that the decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the important thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

Pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Sources indicate that open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

Pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

Pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

In a recent development, the most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

According to recent reports, check your employment contract and tech giant handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

Recent findings suggest that most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

According to recent reports, businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Recent findings suggest that report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Industry observers note that start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP quickly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

Scientists uncover 3 key brain pathways linked to lasting depression relief

📅 18 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1421 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three vital brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments.
  • Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.
  • The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists at Mount Sinai have identified three vital brain connections associated with long-term improvement in patients receiving deep brain stimulation (DBS) for severe depression that has not responded to conventional treatments. The discovery could help researchers make this experimental therapy more precise and effective.

Published October 1 in the American Journal of Psychiatry, the research examined the largest group of patients assembled across multiple independent cohorts to date who had received subcallosal cingulate deep brain stimulation (SCC DBS) for treatment-resistant depression.

The researchers found that lasting improvements were consistently associated with electrical stimulation reaching three specific white matter pathways: the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

These findings strengthen the case for using detailed maps of the brain's connections to determine exactly where electrodes should be implanted, rather than choosing their positions based primarily on anatomical landmarks. Known as connectome-based targeting, this strategy has already helped shape the ongoing Abbott TRANSCEND clinical trial, a randomized, controlled study that uses individualized brain connectivity maps to guide SCC DBS treatment.

"This study underscores the importance of individualized surgical targeting for achieving optimal outcomes with deep brain stimulation for depression," stated Helen Mayberg, MD, Mount Sinai Professor in Neurotherapeutics and founding Director of the Nash Family Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai. "In any randomized controlled trial of a neuromodulation treatment, precise lead placement and confirmation that the intended brain target has been engaged are essential first steps. We still have much to learn about which patients are most likely to benefit from stimulation of this particular target, but developing imaging-based signatures that can match patients to their optimal treatment remains a central goal of our research.".

How Deep Brain Stimulation Targets Severe Depression.

Sources indicate that for people with treatment-resistant depression, standard therapies have failed to provide adequate relief. Researchers are investigating deep brain stimulation as a possible treatment for individuals living with severe, persistent symptoms.

According to recent reports, the procedure involves surgically placing electrodes inside the brain to deliver controlled electrical signals to circuits involved in depression. However, positioning the electrodes correctly remains one of the greatest challenges.

Sources indicate that electrical stimulation does not simply affect the brain tissue closest to an implanted electrode. It can also influence larger networks through the white matter pathways that connect different brain regions. As a result, two patients with electrodes implanted in nearly identical locations may experience very different outcomes depending on which connections are actually stimulated.

Sources indicate that earlier research from Mount Sinai and Emory University helped establish the importance of these networks. In studies published between 2014 and 2023 in Biological Psychiatry, Molecular Psychiatry, and Nature, the teams identified white matter pathways associated with successful SCC DBS treatment and developed a method for planning electrode placement using brain connectivity maps.

The latest investigation sought to determine whether those connections were also crucial in patients treated at other research centers. Scientists also wanted to understand whether differences in the pathways reached by stimulation could help account for patients who did not benefit.

Three Brain Connections Linked to Lasting Improvement.

To investigate, the researchers examined information from several clinical studies, including the BROADEN trial and a patient cohort at the University of Toronto, where SCC DBS was originally developed.

They used computer models of the electrical fields generated by implanted electrodes alongside maps of brain connectivity. This allowed them to estimate which pathways received stimulation and compare those patterns across different patient groups.

The results revealed a consistent relationship between sustained improvement and stimulation of the cingulum bundle, forceps minor, and medial uncinate fasciculus/ventral amygdalofugal pathways.

One finding was especially notable. Across the study sites, patients who had not responded to treatment after two years demonstrated a lack of stimulation engagement with the left cingulum bundle.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers did not investigate whether moving electrodes to reach this pathway would improve those patients' symptoms. Nevertheless, the pattern offers a possible explanation for why apparently similar electrode placements can produce different results. An electrode might be positioned in the correct general region but still fail to activate all the connections associated with lasting improvement.

Sources indicate that "This study addresses an important question in DBS: not simply which area of the brain to stimulate, but which connections within that area need to be engaged," said Brian Kopell, MD, Director of the Center for Neuromodulation at Mount Sinai. "For a network disorder such as depression, millimeters can determine whether stimulation reaches the pathways we intend to modulate. Identifying and reproducibly engaging those pathways gives us a more precise surgical target and a framework for understanding why otherwise similar electrode placements may produce different clinical outcomes.".

Toward More Personalized Depression Treatments.

Although reaching these three pathways appears notable, the researchers emphasize that electrode placement alone is unlikely to determine whether a patient improves.

The investigation concentrated on identifying the brain connections that should receive stimulation. Additional studies are needed to determine which individuals are most likely to benefit from SCC DBS and how electrical stimulation should be adjusted as treatment continues.

There were also limitations to the brain imaging data. Individual diffusion MRI scans, which can provide information about a person's white matter connections, were not available for every participant. Consequently, much of the analysis used generalized maps of brain connectivity rather than maps created specifically for each patient.

It has been revealed that for the Emory patient group, the researchers were able to compare results obtained from generalized connectivity maps with those based on individual diffusion imaging. Both approaches produced consistent findings, providing further support for the importance of the identified pathways. However, more research is needed to establish the value of patient-specific imaging.

Future investigations will explore whether additional brain imaging measurements, including white matter integrity and functional connectivity, can help identify suitable patients, improve electrode placement, and guide treatment settings.

According to recent reports, "Our findings show precisely engaging these white matter pathways is a critical first step toward sustained response," noted Ki Sueng Choi, PhD, Associate Professor, Imaging Core Leader at the Center for Advanced Circuit Therapeutics at Mount Sinai, and corresponding author of the study. "The next step is to characterize abnormal functional and structural brain states along these pathways to build more detailed models for setting patient-specific stimulation parameters, including amplitude, frequency, and pulse width, for precision medicine.".

By combining increasingly detailed brain maps with personalized stimulation settings, scientists hope to better understand why some people experience lasting relief while others do not. The findings represent another step toward developing more targeted treatments for severe depression, although further clinical research is necessary to establish how much these approaches can improve outcomes.

Research Funding and Disclosures.

The research received support from the National Institutes of Health BRAIN Initiative through grant UH3NS103550, the Hope for Depression Research Foundation, and the DANA Foundation.

Abbott's Neuromodulation business supplied data from the BROADEN clinical trial but did not participate in designing or analyzing the current study.
