Latest Update: Five Things Students Taught Us About Connecting Across Differences

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2607 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me.
  • Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors.
  • For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when I’m producing a documentary, one of my favorite parts of the process is the moment when a bit of our footage sticks to me. Permanently. I never know when it will happen, but it always does. The sticky bit could be a snippet of dialogue or a quote from an interview. After watching the footage over and over again, the bit becomes part of me.

Often it’s a funny line—a perfect, punchy distillation of the truth that gets adopted as an inside joke among the team of producers and editors. We repeat it like a collective spell that buoys us when we’re sinking under the weight of the project’s heavy subject matter. Sometimes the thing that sticks is not funny at all. Sometimes it’s a splinter, a cutting insight that I would have rather avoided. Or it’s a solidly true, heartfelt moment that sits like a smooth stone in my pocket. The touchstone grounds and guides me on the long journey of making a film.

For the better part of the past year, I’ve been working as an executive producer on a series of short documentaries for the Greater Good Science Center called Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy. The series features students at four universities across the country who are attempting to connect in some meaningful way with people who have different life experiences, political beliefs, or visions for the future.

It has been revealed that at Iliff School of Theology, master’s and Ph.D. students imagine a version of the United States that embodies their values, and then they share those visions with one another. As they listen to one another’s values, they discover where they align, where they diverge, and where empathy can keep them in relationship with each other even when they disagree.

In a two-part story set at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students from both campuses gather at an event hosted by the schools’ Social Justice Alliance, a first-of-its-kind collaboration between an HBCU (historically Black college or university) and a PWI (predominantly white institution).

At Dickinson College, a deep friendship between the presidents of the Dickinson College Republicans and the Dickinson College Democrats creates the conditions for an unexpectedly collaborative relationship between the two clubs. Members of both clubs gather regularly and listen to each other’s thoughts about complex and often contentious political issues.

Recent findings suggest that back when we were in the middle of editing these episodes with our collaborators at Anaconda Street Productions, I spent an afternoon reviewing footage from one of the shoots, and then I took my dog for a walk. On the walk, I found myself repeating a line from an interview. It stuck! It’s been one of those smooth stones in my pocket ever since.

Industry observers note that of course, I’m not the only one who was changed by the experience of working on this series. To celebrate the release of Connecting on Campus, I invite you behind the scenes to meet my collaborators as we share some of the many things we learned as we helped tell these stories.

Industry observers note that it’s a pretty straightforward message, yet I hear it over and over in my head in the voice of Mrs. Dawn Collins. Your voice matters and everyone has a part to play. Mrs. Collins claims these words during an interview in the first of our two episodes about Bowie State University (BSU) and the University of Maryland (UMD). Mrs. Collins and her husband, Mr. Richard Collins Jr., founded the BSU–UMD Social Justice Alliance after their son, Lt. Richard Collins III, a BSU student, was murdered on the UMD campus by a student in 2017. The Alliance brings together faculty, staff, and students to join the Collins’s commitment to “eradicating the ideology of intolerance, while confronting individuals and combatting systems that normalize indifference, justify injustice, perpetuate hate, and inflict violence.”.

According to recent reports, mrs. Collins’s words have stuck with me, in part, because they insist on every person’s dignity, power, and responsibility. Our voices matter, and we all have a role to play in eradicating the ideology of intolerance and in combatting systems that perpetuate hate and inflict violence. That’s a strong call to action.

Mrs. Collins’s words have also stuck with me because they clearly articulate the heart of this documentary series. The students featured in this series offer us examples of what happens when people step into their power and accept the responsibility to understand themselves, understand each other (differences and all), and work together to build something latest. That new thing could be a collaboration between clubs on campus or a vision for our future as a nation. Either way, these students know their voices matter and they have what it takes to practice doing this work together.

According to recent reports, it was so helpful to have Mrs. Collins’s voice in my head, keeping me anchored in this truth as I worked. — Kelly Rafferty.

When we first imagined Connecting on Campus, we wanted to find places where students were actually practicing the skills and qualities that make connection across differences possible, and to make those moments visible.

Recent findings suggest that as I spent time with these students and their stories, and as we shaped the episodes in the edit, I found myself thinking more and more about choice. Across the series, you see students staying curious when they could shut down, listening to understand someone else’s experience, sharing their own perspective while making space for someone else’s, or finding the courage to remain in a difficult conversation.

In our Dickinson College episode, that choice reveals up in a moment that could have easily passed. Ryan Thies recounts meeting Matthew Craig at a Halloween party during his freshman year. Matthew was dressed as Donald Trump. Ryan could have seen that costume, made an assumption about who Matthew was, and walked away. Instead, he leaned in and got to know him. An unlikely connection became a friendship, and eventually the two chose to become roommates. Ryan’s choice changed what became possible between them. That choice reflects the kind of empathy we talk about in our Bridging Differences work: the deliberate, and often difficult, choice to engage with someone else’s experience even when it feels unfamiliar or challenges our own worldview.

Recent findings suggest that the choices look different in our Bowie State University and University of Maryland episodes—and the stakes are obviously very different, too. Here, the students and the Collins family are stepping into a history that is devastating: the murder of Lt. Richard Collins III on the University of Maryland campus and the work that emerged from it to confront hatred and bring students from the two campuses together.

Here, courage looks like choosing to show up and engage when discomfort, conflict, and fear might make it easier—and completely understandable—to withdraw. It’s the decision to say: This matters. I’ll attend. I’ll represent. I’ll listen. I’ll do my part.

Practices like “Listen with Empathy,” “Understand Their Values,” “Expand Your Views and Circles,” or “Perspective Giving and Getting” from our Bridging Differences in Higher Education Playbook can be learned.

But the choice to engage is one each of us has to make. My hope is that people watch these stories asking themselves, “What did that person do that made greater understanding possible, and where might I try that myself?”  — Juliana Tafur.

I came away thinking that “bridging” is sometimes misunderstood as compromise. Across all four videos, something more interesting emerges: You can build a relationship across a difference without necessarily resolving the difference itself.

According to recent reports, at Iliff School of Theology, students imagine very different versions of America without being asked to arrive at one shared vision. At Dickinson, Republicans and Democrats engage seriously with each other without abandoning their political beliefs. And at Bowie State University and the University of Maryland, students move beyond assumptions, allow themselves to be vulnerable, ask difficult questions, and really listen to people whose backgrounds and experiences differ from their own. The circumstances are very different, but the lesson is consistent: Bridging isn’t about erasing what separates us. It’s about developing the curiosity, trust, and courage to stay connected across those differences.

The series asks a harder and more useful question than “How do we get everyone to agree?” It asks how we live, learn, and build community with people who may never see the world exactly as we do. The answers aren’t presented as a formula. You get to watch people experiment with listening, vulnerability, curiosity, disagreement, and repair, then decide for yourself what actually works. — Omar Lugones.

Recent findings suggest that in my own experiences in smaller, more intimate classroom settings, I often observe an echo-chamber effect when opinions are shared, especially when the class is discussing a controversial topic. I have noticed a general apprehension about “going first” or initiating the conversation. Speaking for myself, I am often afraid of offering the “wrong” opinion, meaning a perspective that could be interpreted as supporting a politically or socially unacceptable position and cause my peers to view me as an outsider. I do not necessarily think my peers are experiencing the exact same thought process, but I sense that they are also self-conscious about expressing a conflicting opinion. As a result, people may default to agreeing with whoever offers an opinion first.

I thought it was remarkable that at Iliff School of Theology, Lindsay Ambler and Stephanie Nelson initially disagree with one another, and that moment opens space for others to enter the conversation and offer their own perspectives. By disagreeing respectfully, they demonstrate how disagreement can produce a deeper understanding of an issue than a conversation built only around agreement.

Industry observers note that lindsay takes a strong position on the effects of religion based on her past experiences with Christian institutions. By sharing an extremely vulnerable personal story, she creates the conditions for others to share their experiences and, in turn, promotes a greater sense of empathy within the conversation.

Sources indicate that when Stephanie offers her own perspective on whether society can reach a state of perfection and equality, her response conflicts with Lindsay’s position. This point of contention could seemingly disrupt the vulnerable environment Lindsay has created, yet it does not. Instead, Lindsay responds to the challenge by deepening her explanation. In doing so, she creates upcoming points of entry for others to join the conversation and contribute their own experiences.

At the end of the discussion, Stephanie expresses gratitude to those who shared their perspectives and revealed gaps in her own thinking. The conversation demonstrates how respectful disagreement can foster empathy, growth, and greater participation from every member of a group. — Tyler C. Tang.

In a recent development, working on this series, I noticed the relationship between character and discomfort. Courage, empathy, humility, and curiosity all sound admirable in the abstract, but you really discover whether you possess them when another person challenges you. Character in these films often reveals itself in what someone does immediately after hearing something they don’t agree with.

For example, I identified with Josh Perez, a Ph.D. student and teaching assistant at Iliff School of Theology, in particular. I appreciate the way he draws on his own experiences as a second-generation Mexican American while recognizing that other people carry struggles he may never experience himself. His vision isn’t simply about creating a world that works better for people like him. It’s about making room for others to find liberation from their own struggles, as well. That ability to be grounded in your own experience while still making space for the experiences of others is at the heart of bridging differences. — Antonio Carrasco III.

If you’re exhausted by watching people argue about politics, identity, and social issues, watch people actually talk to each other instead. The series doesn’t suggest that differences disappear when people sit down together. It shows that disagreement can be productive when people approach each other with curiosity and humility.

According to recent reports, iliff School of Theology student Lindsay Ambler’s story affected me in a way I didn’t expect. It was hard to hear how painful some of her experiences within religious spaces had been. Learning how she was rejected after people discovered she was gay gave me a much deeper understanding of what she carried into the classroom. It reminded me how little we may know about someone until we give them the space to share their story.

Logan Midler from the University of Maryland stands out to me, too. I appreciate how honest she is about not having much interaction with people from different backgrounds and how easy it can be to start those conversations. Her desire to listen, learn, and become a better ally feels like a simple yet powerful example of bridging differences. — Ryan Carrasco.

I hope there’s a moment in Connecting on Campus that sticks with you, too. Maybe that memorable line, that bit of dialogue, or that mindful pause will become a touchstone for your own experiments in bridging differences.

As another academic year begins, may the stories in this series also serve as an example of what students are capable of doing when they’re given the space and support to practice connecting with one another. Campuses across the country are facing real challenges—everything from threats of censorship to rising costs and cuts to funding—and these opportunities to practice bridging differences must not be sacrificed along the way. They’re too vital to our individual and collective well-being.

Watch Connecting on Campus: Stories of Courage, Curiosity, and Empathy.

#138772. You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1679 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Berkeley ↗ Open Full Page

You Might Be Experiencing Rustout, Not Burnout, at Work

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1679 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent.
  • Industry observers note that it’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves.
  • Industry observers note that rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some forms of distress at work are easy to recognize because they interrupt someone’s daily performance and the work of those around them: For example, a person on your team becomes visibly exhausted, they are irritable, or they’re frequently absent. But other forms of distress are harder to see precisely because the work continues uninterrupted.

Industry observers note that it’s common to talk about burnout at work and to recognize it in others and in ourselves. But a new paper of mine with David S. Smith examines a less visible and less understood form of disengagement at work: rustout.

Industry observers note that rustout, as we studied it, often involves being underutilized, intellectually stagnating, and feeling a deep-seated sense of unfulfillment. It can arise when people feel their work no longer offers enough meaning or challenge to keep them intellectually and creatively engaged. But because it’s different from burnout, the solutions are also different—both for individuals and for organizations.

I’ve presented this research at numerous conferences, and each time I have been approached by professionals who say, “That’s what I’ve been going through, but I never had a name for it until now.”.

Industry observers note that these people, young and older, are committed to their work, they are hardworking, and they haven’t stopped caring. It is often the case that they care very much, and they meet expectations set before them. They are often the ones who are called upon because they are reliable and highly conscientious.

If you look around your workplace, you probably know many people who fit this bill. The problem is not a loss of effort on the part of the individual; it is a breakdown in the relationship between effort and meaningful work. From my study of this topic, rustout is really about the decline in professional vitality, when a person’s capacities are not used in ways that feel meaningful to them.

It has been revealed that in our research, participants described experiences shaped by administrative overload, reduced autonomy, and a misalignment between their professional aspirations and assigned tasks. Many people highlighted feeling professionally stuck: “Sadly, the elements I love about the job . . . are often overshadowed by the other administrative aspects of the role,” “I feel like I’m feeding the machine,” and “I’m a square peg in a round hole.”.

Recent findings suggest that they highlighted a sense that the work they were doing no longer drew sufficiently on their talents: “The better you are at it, the more of the administrative side of the job you get. It’s lacking opportunities to be creative.”.

Rustout can be quite psychologically disorienting. From the outside, a person may appear successful and competent. There is no question about their productivity; they meet set targets, but could do so “with [their] eyes closed.” However, they may feel increasingly detached from the work that once animated them. Their distress isn’t dramatic; it’s a slow process of psychological erosion.

In many ways, rustout overlaps with burnout, but they are not the same. Burnout involves prolonged negative stress that isn’t adequately managed. It’s about too much—working too much, caring too much, too much pressure, and too little time to recuperate. In contrast, rustout is associated with too little positive stress or challenge over time, too little stimulation, and limited opportunities for individual growth.

However, while burnout is part of organizations’ mental health literacy, rustout rarely gets a mention. And this is problematic—both for the individual and the organization. “I often feel I have produced nothing at the end of the week, and there is no sense of development,” one person said.

Some will stay in their roles out of a sense of duty (and for other practical reasons like salary or seniority), but others will choose to leave. Another remarked, “I am functioning at my job, but I’m not thriving, and I am looking elsewhere.”.

In a recent development, rustout often hides behind competence, and the reliable person is often given more of the same work. The person who does not complain is assumed to be coping and doing OK. The person who stabilizes others and is a good team player is rarely asked whether they themselves feel developed or challenged.

Recent findings suggest that one person mentioned, “I have no experience of ever having a conversation with anyone around it. No line manager ever named it, it has never been mentioned in a communal setting or in a one-to-one setting. . . . No one has ever asked, ‘Do you feel fulfilled or do you feel you have opportunities to use your skills and talents in a meaningful way?’”.

According to recent reports, it’s easy to see how doing overtime and being dependable can become a trap. Eventually, the employee becomes valued less for what they might become and more for what they can continue to absorb—they won’t “rock the boat” by opening the can of worms that is their dissatisfaction. “You put up, and shut up,” one person mentioned.

Boost satisfaction, engagement, and collaboration with this three-course series.

Meanwhile, many workplaces are organized to detect individual or team shortcomings (or failure) more readily than stagnation. If someone stops performing, the problem becomes visible. However, if someone continues to perform while becoming inwardly disengaged, the organization may see no problem at all. And if anyone notices their dissatisfaction, they may not openly discuss it, as another of my interviewees reported. “It suits everyone not to talk about it; when everyone is working and doing their jobs—then don’t disturb anything. Everything is cosy.”.

Participants experiencing rustout described barriers that limited their ability to use their strengths or pursue professional growth, which are particularly vital for having a sense of meaning and fulfillment at work.

For many people, their working life gives them a sense of identity and purpose, but when work no longer offers that sense of meaning, their relationship with the job can become fractured or feel “off.” In some cases, they can’t put their finger on what is happening, and that might be why I often hear after presentations, “I never had a name for it.”.

Industry observers note that naming rustout won’t solve the matter, but it can help the person to understand why they feel underutilized or dissatisfied. Naming rustout can help people understand this isn’t a personal failure but an experience that is shaped by the design or conditions of work (much like burnout). It is also shaped by the culture of work, particularly when there is a resistance to change or a failure to see the value in helping people to flourish.

From my discussions with participants and colleagues about rustout, it is clear that it isn’t a pre-retirement phenomenon. It seems to arise for those who are experienced, perhaps mid-career, and those who have been in their role for a long time.

Industry observers note that one participant explained, “I have been doing [this role] for years. There must be better ways to organize things to ensure the expertise of experienced staff is used in more effective ways.” Others said, “It’s the seven-, eight-, nine-year mark when there isn’t an opportunity to be stimulated,” and “It’s the seven-year itch, you’ve been doing something creative and then you reach a point where you are doing the same thing on repeat.”.

Sources indicate that in such ways, we can’t dismiss rustout as a consequence of aging in the workplace. It can happen whenever people are pigeonholed into a system that no longer offers them meaningful development. Although some repetition and routine are an expected part of every job, there should also be a sense that your abilities and talents matter in your role. That there is a future and something exciting to work toward.

Industry observers note that the language of burnout has helped many people name distress that had previously been normalized or dismissed. It has also helped organizations take workplace well-being more seriously. But any dominant mental health vocabulary can become limiting when it starts to stand in for the whole field of experience. If burnout is the only category available for occupational distress, then recovery is often imagined in terms of rest and resilience.

They may be necessary, but they are not always sufficient. A person experiencing rustout may not simply need less work; they may need different work: work that restores their sense of intellectual engagement and curiosity. As Maya Angelou once said, “We aren’t designed to be static”—that could apply to all aspects of life, including the workplace.

If you are experiencing rustout, it would be good to do an inventory of what is happening for you. Do you feel fulfilled in your role? Do you have opportunities to use your talents? Do you gain some sense of meaning from your role? Are there ways to seek renewal in your work? What might this look like, and can you have this conversation with your line manager or boss?

For organizations, the questions are also direct. Look around your team. Are you giving your most dependable employees opportunities for development? Do you continually lean on their “safe pair of hands” because it is easier than asking someone else to learn the ropes? Are you willing to put the conversation about professional dissatisfaction on the table? How can you help your team to flourish?

That is the unsettling truth at the heart of the rustout. A person can be conscientious yet disengaged, reliable yet underused, competent but unfulfilled. They can be good at their job and still feel themselves receding from it. The silence around rustout allows it to thrive, which is why I often hear the same response after conference presentations: “I thought it was just me.” I think there is a particular loneliness in that sentence, the loneliness of continuing to do the work, while privately wondering why it no longer feels like yours.

It has been revealed that sabrina Fitzsimons, Ph.D., is a lecturer at Dublin City University, Ireland. Her research combines expertise in educators’ occupational well-being, mental health, and online environments.

Latest Update: Scientists discover a surprising secret behind the human brain’s wrinkles

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1061 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves.
  • Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans.
  • Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most primates have relatively large brains covered in distinctive folds and grooves. However, common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus) are an unusual exception. These small monkeys have brains that are almost entirely smooth, with very little folding. Scientists at the German Primate Center (DPZ), the Leibniz Institute for Primate Research in Göttingen, have now identified several cellular processes that help explain this difference.

Using miniature brain structures known as organoids, the researchers discovered that certain neural progenitor cells, which produce neurons, develop differently in marmosets than in humans. These differences involve the cells' structure, the speed at which they divide, and the timing of their development. Together, these changes reduce the number of neurons produced, contributing to the smaller size and smoother surface of the marmoset brain. Published in Science Advances, the findings provide latest insights into primate brain evolution and could eventually improve our understanding of human brain development disorders.

Why Some Primate Brains Are Smooth Instead of Folded.

Brain size and the extent of surface folding are vital features that distinguish different primate species. The human brain, for example, has a highly folded surface resembling the ridges and grooves of a walnut. This arrangement greatly expands the brain's surface area, creating room for billions of neurons that support complex thinking and other advanced mental abilities.

According to recent reports, scientists believe that the common ancestor of modern primates already possessed a moderately sized brain with at least some folding. Yet not all primates living today retain these characteristics.

Common marmosets (Callithrix jacchus), small monkeys native to South America that are becoming increasingly important in biomedical research, have brains with almost no visible folds. Researchers at the German Primate Center set out to determine why their brains develop so differently from those of humans and other primates.

According to recent reports, "We wanted to understand which changes at the cellular level cause the marmoset brain to grow less and form fewer folds," explains Lidiia Tynianskaia, one of the study's two first authors and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution at the DPZ. "At the beginning of development, the common marmoset brain exhibits the typical structure and composition of a large, folded primate brain. As development progresses, processes must therefore occur that effectively slow down the production of nerve cells.".

Scientists Discover What Slows Brain Growth.

It has been revealed that to investigate these developmental differences, the team compared brain organoids grown from human and common marmoset cells. Their attention centered on neural progenitor cells, the cells responsible for generating neurons during brain development.

Recent findings suggest that these progenitor cells play a major role in determining the eventual size and shape of the brain. The more neurons they produce, the greater the potential for the cerebral cortex to expand and develop folds.

According to recent reports, the researchers found that the marmoset's smaller, smoother cerebral cortex is not the result of a single developmental change. Instead, several differences involving distinct types of progenitor cells work together to limit neuron production and brain folding.

In a recent development, "Our investigations have shown that certain progenitor cells in the common marmoset divide significantly more slowly than in humans," explains César Mateo Bastidas Betancourt, also a first author of the study and a PhD student in the Junior Research Group. "Other progenitor cells have a simpler structure than their human counterparts, with fewer processes, and are therefore less proliferative. Both of these factors ultimately result in fewer nerve cells, which contributes to a smaller size and less folding of the cerebral cortex in marmosets.".

It has been revealed that the scientists also identified crucial differences in when certain progenitor cell characteristics and behaviors emerge during development. Compared with humans, marmosets have a shorter overall period during which these cells can multiply rapidly.

Together, the slower rate of cell division, simpler cell structures, and shorter window for rapid growth help explain why the marmoset brain produces fewer neurons and develops far fewer folds.

Miniature Brains Reveal Vital Developmental Clues.

Sources indicate that much of the research relied on brain organoids, small, three-dimensional structures grown from cells that reproduce important features of early brain development. These miniature models allowed scientists to investigate developmental changes across multiple samples and compare the timing of key processes.

It has been revealed that "The study combines the advantages of in vivo and in vitro methods," notes Michael Heide, head of the Junior Research Group Brain Development and Evolution. "Organoids are well-suited for obtaining statistically robust results because such sample sizes are not feasible in primates. We subsequently repeated some key experiments in fetal brain tissue to confirm the results from the organoids.".

Recent findings suggest that one particularly notable finding involved the relationship between development in organoids and development in actual marmoset brains. The researchers determined that a marmoset brain organoid grown for 50 days closely matches the developmental stage of a natural marmoset brain at day 90.

Sources indicate that establishing this relationship was essential because brain organoids and actual brains do not necessarily develop at the same rate. By identifying corresponding developmental stages, the scientists could make meaningful comparisons and interpret their experimental findings more reliably.

What Smooth Monkey Brains Reveal About Human Brain Evolution.

The findings help explain how relatively small differences in the behavior and developmental timing of brain-building cells can contribute to major differences in brain size and folding among primates.

They also offer a potential explanation for how the wide variety of primate brain shapes and sizes emerged over evolutionary time, including why some species developed relatively smooth brains while others possess much larger, heavily folded ones.

Beyond their evolutionary significance, these discoveries provide a foundation for investigating how the human brain develops and what happens when those processes are disrupted. A better understanding of the cellular mechanisms that control neuron production and brain growth could ultimately help researchers study developmental disorders affecting the human brain.

Tech Report: Can Community Programs Reduce Gun Violence?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.
  • This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years.
  • According to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study by researchers at UC Berkeley’s Center for Global Healthy Cities published in the Journal of the American Medical Association Network Open found that the California city of Richmond’s Office of Neighborhood Safety (ONS) was responsible for a 61% reduction in that city’s firearm homicides and injury shootings over the last 14 years.

This is one of the only studies in the country to document the sustained impacts of a community violence intervention program on city-wide firearm violence over more than 10 years.

According to lead author Alice Bruno, a doctoral student in epidemiology at UC Berkeley’s School of Public Health, “we leveraged data from dozens of comparable cities across the United States to estimate what firearm violence would have looked like in Richmond without the ONS, Peacemaker Fellowship. We found that the Fellowship contributed to long-term reductions in violence, and that the declines only grew as the program operated.” Other UC Berkeley coauthors include Jason Corburn; Mahasin Mujahid, chair of the Division of Epidemiology; Sean Darling-Hammond; and Juan Cabrera.

Sam Vaughn, director of ONS, said, “The statistics back up what we have seen in the streets: fewer shootings, fewer deaths, and a healthier community overall.”.

Recent findings suggest that homicide rates are down across the country; the FBI recently released data showing murder rates are down a record 18.1% nationally. However, Richmond has consistently outperformed national declines for over a decade, suggesting the results are due to that city’s innovative, street-outreach interventions and their mentorship of active firearm offenders, a program called Operation Peacemaker Fellowship, which was instituted in 2010. The Fellowship uses a public health approach to preventing gun violence.

According to James Houston, the program manager of the ONS who oversees the day-to-day implementation of the Peacemaker Fellowship, including managing 14 street-outreach workers who right now serve 123 participants, “the credit goes to the young people making better decisions and the team that gives them support, mentorship, and encouragement every day to make a change.”.

According to recent reports, according to Shasa Curl, Richmond city manager, Richmond had over 300 police officer full-time equivalent in 2014 and 180 in 2020, but was down to 121 active sworn officers by 2024. Yet during this time, the ONS, through continued city support and grants, was able to expand its staff and increase the number of fellows and participants. Even during the COVID-19 period, the study shows Richmond did not have as significant a spike in firearm violence as most cities did across the Bay Area and nationally.

According to the ONS, the health impacts are lives saved, safer streets, and community members with a renewed positive life outlook.

According to recent reports, one former Peacemaker Fellowship participant said, “Before the ONS came to me, I didn’t care if I survived past 19, as long as I had a name in the streets. After my experience with the ONS, with my mentor coming at me every day, I got support for my stress, got a job, paying my bills, and have a kid now. I’m no longer terrorizing my community.”.

The paper notes the cascading health benefits for entire communities when gun violence reductions are sustained, such as the case in Richmond. Further research will explore how unique aspects of the ONS might be contributing to declines in gun violence, including that the program is a city government agency, independent from the police department, has had consistent funding, has trained and retained many of the same outreach workers for over a decade (these city staff are well paid with benefits), and delivers individualized supports to each participant based on their needs, such as food and housing assistance, cognitive behavioral therapy, addiction and anger management counseling, and other social services aimed at both reducing gun violence risk and addressing trauma.

This article was originally published on Berkeley Public Health News. Read the original article.

UC Berkeley School of Public Health has been a global health leader in research innovation, educational excellence, and social impact for more than 75 years.

#138769. How Love Saves Lives

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3358 w)

How Love Saves Lives

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3358 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When someone takes his own life, the grief of parents, lovers, children, and friends can be unspeakable.
  • How could this talented, beautiful young person not know she’d be terribly, horribly missed?
  • Most experts attribute suicide to severe mental illness caused by a brain injury or genetic predisposition, or due to some other, as yet unknown, physical or chemical trigger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When someone takes his own life, the grief of parents, lovers, children, and friends can be unspeakable. At a memorial for one young suicide I attended a few years ago, the father of the deceased could barely walk to the altar to light a candle. Everyone was crying.

How could this talented, beautiful young person not know she’d be terribly, horribly missed?

Most experts attribute suicide to severe mental illness caused by a brain injury or genetic predisposition, or due to some other, as yet unknown, physical or chemical trigger. Severe depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia are all inordinately common among people who die by suicide.

Severe mental illnesses are no doubt responsible for many, if not most, of the eight hundred thousand or so suicides that occur around the world each year, including, perhaps, that young person’s whose memorial I attended.

Sources indicate that my book, Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic, isn’t primarily about such cases—or about how to prevent suicide. Such a book would have detailed sections about psychotherapy, restrictions on firearms, safety barriers for bridges, and other measures that really do save lives. Instead, my aim was to explore why some people want to take their own lives in the first place and how that desire might be reduced, in both individuals and communities.

It has been revealed that having spent the past few years reading about suicide, speaking with scores of people who’ve experienced suicidal feelings, and having experienced them myself from time to time, I’ve come to understand that what suicidal people feel is the indifference, not of the universe, but of those closest to them. They sense that their own feelings don’t matter to the people they care most about.

These experiences are backed up by studies showing that the main reason suicidal people want to die is because they think no one cares about them. Some suicides even seem to believe they’re doing everyone a favor by taking their own lives.

Psychologist Thomas Joiner, who’s been studying suicide for thirty years, calls it a force of nature that distorts people’s minds so they become convinced that they are a burden to others and no one wants them around. In study after study, the most common trigger for suicide is a perceived rupture in a close relationship, either with a lover, parent, or other close relative, that seems irreparable to the suicidal person.

In a recent development, given that suicide seems driven by fraught or broken connections, it’s perhaps not surprising that I also discovered that suicide can spread within social groups like a disease. The suicide rate of particular groups can jump—sometimes increasing three- or four-fold or more—in a short time, meaning it behaves like an epidemic, like malaria during the rainy season or flu in the fall. Suicide epidemics unfold more slowly than these microbial plagues—over years or decades, not weeks or months—but they happen far too quickly to result from genetic changes, and affect far too many people to be explained away as spontaneous cases of biologically caused mental illness or brain injury. The causes therefore must have something to do with the changing social environment in which these people live. Suicide epidemics have occurred on virtually every continent.

Recent findings suggest that what’s scary about this is that it means suicide could come for any of us. The very existence of suicide epidemics proves that people with suicidal feelings aren’t a species apart. Anyone can feel suicidal under certain conditions—and the key to stopping suicide epidemics is to change those conditions.

According to recent reports, I teach and write about public health and have long been fascinated by epidemics because they always tell a story. In most literary depictions of epidemics, such as Albert Camus’s The Plague or Daniel Defoe’s A Journal of the Plague Year, they seem to strike from nowhere, but this isn’t how epidemics typically behave. Individual cases of disease are hard to predict. Some of us will become ill tomorrow, but there’s no telling who. Even those who take risks may well escape the consequences.

What might cause a suicide epidemic?

First, it’s important to understand what doesn’t. Suicide isn’t more common during wars or where people are poorer or have recently experienced some environmental disaster like a flood, earthquake, or wildfire. Suicide was common among African slaves, especially on the ships en route to America and when they first arrived, but despite segregation, police brutality, mass incarceration, and other outrages, the suicide rate of African Americans has been generally lower than that of U.S. whites since record-keeping began in the 1930s.

What seems to matter is whether people believe someone, somewhere, really cares about and understands them.

Industry observers note that the mental pain that drives suicide is really the flip side of love, indicates Israeli neuroscientist Yoram Yovell. “It probably evolved along with motherhood. . . . Inherent in us are very strong emotional forces that function to keep mothers and babies together. When they get too far from each other, they feel mental pain,” which we experience when we search for love. This is why “so many children’s stories are about a boy looking for his lost mother.”.

Evidence supports Yovell’s theory. A 1999 study found that some 78% of high lethality suicide attempters had recently experienced the loss of a close personal relationship, and suicide notes often express love for those left behind. In 2012, Zimri Yaseen and his colleagues reported that suicidal people interviewed in emergency rooms were especially likely to report that in the three preceding days, they’d felt “unusually intense or deep feelings of love,” which they presumably also felt were not reciprocated.

But why would large groups of people—from the islands of Micronesia to the Arctic Circle, from the cities of post-communist Russia to the towns of contemporary America—suddenly begin questioning their most intimate attachments? How does love suddenly disappear—or seem to—from the lives of thousands of people?

In my book, Why Live, I argue that it has to do with how we internalize socioeconomic change.

The first well-researched suicide epidemic occurred across Western Europe during the 19th century. Intellectuals debated the causes as we debate the vicissitudes of the stock market. Rising suicide rates were attributed to socialism, atmospheric moisture, the vice of masturbation, and the Romantic era inclination to preserve—through death—the passions of youth against the onslaught of Bourgeois boredom brought on by industrialization and urban life.

Doctors even searched, in vain, for a “suicidogenic” organ in the cadavers of people who’d died by suicide. But others blamed society, that collective property of human groups that shapes our thinking and behavior.

Sources indicate that as a Jew growing up in France amid increasing anti-Semitism, Émile Durkheim had seen how shared values and beliefs buffered his people against the effects of discrimination and how anti-Semitism tightened bonds among them. He went on to become one of the founders of sociology, which is the study of those bonds: what holds us together, what drives us apart, and what happens as a result.

In a recent development, in his 1897 book, Suicide, Durkheim theorized that suicides increase wherever society is fragmenting and people are growing more detached from one another: where divorce rates are higher, for example, and where Protestants, with their individualistic culture and aloofness from collective ritual, outnumber Catholics. He likened it to entropy—the universal tendency toward chaos and disorder at the atomic level discovered by physicists earlier in the century. Appearing on the eve of humanity’s, as yet, bloodiest century, Durkheim’s book seemed to foreshadow the trouble to come.

What is it about fragmenting societies that causes mental pain?

In a recent development, durkheim was vague, even a little loopy, when it came to explaining this. At the time, psychologists were just discovering the unconscious, which they explored through studies of hypnosis and hallucinations. Durkheim followed this research closely, and believed that values and meanings flowed through populations like electrical currents, as if societies had what scholars Laurent Mucchielli and Marc Renneville refer to as a “collective soul.” These currents could change people’s behavior through unconscious mechanisms, just as changes in temperature and pressure change the behavior of molecules.

Many late-19th-century scientists believed that our brains generated signals analogous to radio waves. Alexander Graham Bell, Nikola Tesla, and James Clerk Maxwell even wired up helmets and other gizmos to try to measure them. Mark Twain told Harper’s Monthly that thoughts could shoot from brain to brain, without their owners having to open their mouths to communicate. Likewise, Durkheim maintained that whatever suicidal people said about their feelings were just expressions of resolutions planted in their minds by the vibes of a disintegrating society.

In a recent development, the brain-wave theory eventually fell out of fashion. In the 1930s, one of Durkheim’s protégés came closer to explaining the psychological effects of social fragmentation. Maurice Halbwachs taught at the University of Strasbourg from 1919 until his death in a Nazi concentration camp in 1945. His 1930 monograph The Causes of Suicide identified an existential loneliness that, if not entirely new, flourished in the growing towns and cities of 19th-century Europe and the countryside they engulfed.

According to Halbwachs, cities create opportunities for social and economic advancement, but they also create the conditions for exploitative relationships, swindles, romantic betrayals, fragile friendships, broken families, unstable jobs, and many other sources of despair.

Sources indicate that as European cities grew, so did a new class of people who were particularly prone to suicide, including abandoned lovers, lonely widowers, workers who’d lost their jobs, nobles shamed by some dishonorable act, gamblers who couldn’t pay their debts, merchants who’d ruined themselves, heirs who’d squandered their fortunes, and others who’d suffered a common bitter fate: sudden exclusion from a cherished social community. As Halwachs writes:.

Sources indicate that they all see their social level lowered. They are to a certain extent declassed. But what does it mean to be declassed? It is to pass from a group that one knows, that esteems you, to another that ignores you and whose appreciation one has no reason to hold. One then feels a void opening around oneself. Those who once surrounded you, with whom you had so many ideas in common, so many prejudices in common, with whom so many affinities brought you together because you found yourself in them as they found yourself in you, suddenly move away. You disappear from their concerns and their memory. Those among whom you find yourself understand neither your disorientation, nor your nostalgia and your regrets. Detached from the group by a sudden shock, you are incapable, or at least you believe yourself incapable, of ever finding in another any support, nor anything to replace what you have lost.

Industry observers note that in the midst of the 19th-century suicide crisis, the very meaning of the word “lonely” changed, from an adjective typically used to describe empty places and people who stood alone before God to one with the emotional and psychological connotations it has for us today. Suicidal despair, Halbwachs wrote, had been rarer in the past because traditional rural life was simpler and more predictable:.

We lived on the spot . . . adapted to each other, knowing each other too well to be frequently exposed to the clashes that occur when we move from one place, one situation, one profession, to another. Business carried less risk. Ambitions were less aroused, humiliations rarer. We thought and felt in common. Sorrows and troubles, instead of concentrating within the consciousness of this or that individual, dispersed and died out within the group.

What Halbwachs was describing was the transition from what German sociologist Ferdinand Tönnies called Gemeinschaft, or communities based on trust, mutual respect, and sharing of whatever material goods one had, to Gesellschaft, societies based largely on market transactions and political calculation in which ties of friendship and loyalty are relegated to private family life, and may not even reliably be found there.

As far as I’ve been able to determine, wherever that transition has occurred, a suicide epidemic has followed swiftly behind.

But there is another ingredient, too. As villagers shifted away from subsistence and small-scale farming to wage labor and trade, their intimate relationships became both more fragile and more precious. The extended family, which once formed a social mesh that supported everyone, waned in significance, and walls rose up around increasingly private and nuclearized families, usually dominated by a single, generally male breadwinner, upon whom everyone else in the family depended. If you felt your family didn’t respect and care about you, you were in a new sort of trouble, not just because the community no longer offered you a livelihood, but because your whole identity was at stake.

Modern capitalist society creates, in all of us, something of the double consciousness described by the great African American sociologist W. E. B. DuBois. When a modern person looks at a stranger, he wonders not only, as his villager ancestors did, “What can I do to help this person? And is he the kind of person who will help me?” but “What does that stranger see when he looks at me? What essence does he detect? A beauty or a beast? A success or a failure? A respectable person or a fool?”.

The answer sometimes comes as a disappointment. In traditionally cohesive societies, this mattered less, because a person’s worth was measured by what he did for others, and everyone was capable of contributing something. You might not be the best hunter, fisherman, storyteller, or drummer; you might not be the best grower of breadfruit or builder of igloos; but you still mattered. Only the greedy and selfish were looked down upon and excluded.

In modern societies, generosity still counts, but for far less than it used to. If others find us wanting—because of our looks, talents, graces, bank accounts, intelligence, or for whatever reason—we are alone with it, and must make sense of it, somehow.

Sources indicate that for most of us, what makes modern life, with all its loneliness and insecurity, bearable are close relationships with people we count on to see and accept us for who we really are—whatever our flaws. Romantic rejection is exquisitely painful because we feel that that special quality within us, the thing that makes us lovable—and everyone has something—has either been unrecognized or, worse, seen and rejected.

It has been revealed that the pain of rejection by a parent or other close relative is even worse because it can make us feel as though no one could ever understand and sympathize with us. After all, they know us best of all.

In the absence of an abstract sense of group belonging, interpersonal love, especially between parents and children and romantic partners, has become the main source of our psychological resilience, our ability to withstand the disappointments encountered in the outside world, just as the mutually reinforcing group gave strength to our ancestors fighting for survival on the plains, tundras, beaches, and forests of the past.

Love is not just a feeling; it’s also a culture, which developed fairly recently, first in Western societies, and then around the world on the heels of capitalism, modernity, and individualism. It’s no coincidence, the social philosopher Erich Fromm pointed out, that as modern ways of life displaced the traditional, cohesive village and clan, love poems, songs, and stories came to occupy the center of Western culture, displacing archaic tales of heroism and godliness.

Sources indicate that it’s not that love was absent from the art of the ancient past, but as often as not, it was seen as a cause of calamity and human folly. Think of Helen of Troy, Dido and Aeneas, Adam and Eve. Then, more or less in lockstep with commercial culture and urbanization, love came to be seen as a force superior to the gods or God or honor or historic destiny.

The behavior of parents and spouses changed, too. Until the 1800s, childrearing in England, for example, was seen as an exercise less in nurturing than in training for adulthood. Men who were fed up with their wives could sell them at markets or abandon them and marry someone else without divorcing. Infants who died weren’t even listed in parish registers. Only in the 19th century did heartfelt observations of sons and daughters begin appearing regularly in the diaries of American and English mothers.

With the growth of markets and formal state institutions, people came to rely less on kinship networks for social welfare and trade and the family gradually shifted from an economic enterprise to a child-centered haven in a heartless world. The 1700s saw the first toy shops, women’s magazines, popular child care manuals, and family portraits. Christian churches, which had previously stressed family discipline and sometimes even the virtues of wife-beating, now promoted ideals of conjugal and parental love.

In a recent development, today, birthday parties, children’s allowances, and Valentine’s Day cards are symbols we use to assure each other that our most notable relationships are real. Meanwhile, parenting manuals, happily-ever-after fairy tales, Hollywood movies, and the novels of Jane Austen, George Eliot, Charles Dickens, Barbara Cartland, Colleen Hoover, and countless others illustrate the enactment of love according to Western norms.

Industry observers note that premodern Europeans, as well as Indigenous groups the world over, didn’t need this culture because in the mutual aid communities of bygone days, you knew who you were and what you needed to do to gain the esteem of others: You had to pitch in for the group. You helped others and they helped you. That was love, and according to accounts of anthropologists, it was everywhere, as ubiquitous as air.

Recent findings suggest that but when these groups modernized, in some cases very rapidly under the forces of capitalism and colonialism, the rules changed. Now it was unclear what the common goals were and what others were looking for in us. If they didn’t like us, there wasn’t a lot we could do about it. If the people we loved—our romantic partners, parents, and children—felt that way, it was intolerably painful because our hearts had nowhere to turn. Every rejection could now elicit devastating feelings of aloneness. “Who am I?” we are left to wonder. “Am I worth anything at all to anyone?”.

According to recent reports, signifiers of love—birthday cards and so on—aren’t enough. We need the confidence that our own feelings are understood. Some people, either because of the distortions of mental illness or because they really are lost and alone, simply don’t have it.

But all is not lost. As I argue in Why Live, communities can regrow, just like decimated forests. The best policy I can think of is to strive for greater economic equality, which will naturally reduce insecurity, and, in turn, foster greater spiritual as well as material generosity. We are kinder to one another when we don’t feel threatened. Otherwise, the best advice I can think of is not to make things worse. When positive communities begin to emerge, the trick is not to ruin them.

Let’s treat communities like ecosystems so that every time a major economic policy shift is proposed—a massive upcoming trade deal or development project—the effects on communities are considered, and the preservation of Gemeinschaft is prioritized. Ideally, studies of this, analogous to the environmental impact studies now required by all World Bank loans to developing countries, would be conducted with the full and meaningful involvement of affected communities.

In a recent development, some elements of Gemeinschaft survive, even in these harsh times—in well-functioning neighborhoods, in friendship networks, sometimes in the military, and in some schools and workplaces. You know it when you see it; it’s where you feel your dignity is recognized. In defending and building that, we give everyone more reason to live.

In a recent development, helen C. Epstein, Ph.D., is visiting professor of global public health and human rights at Bard College. She is the author of Why Live: How Suicide Becomes an Epidemic and Another Fine Mess: America, Uganda, and the War on Terror.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, noted at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

It has been revealed that the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

It has been revealed that the second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

Recent findings suggest that A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

In a recent development, among the night’s other massive-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

According to recent reports, arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a new auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

Tech Report: In the Face of Crisis, Psychologists Urge a Return to the Basics

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1338 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by new technology, global crises, and loneliness.
  • Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing.
  • Industry observers note that the field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As numerous surveys suggest, people today often feel overwhelmed by new technology, global crises, and loneliness. What do the nation’s psychologists recommend? At the annual convention of the American Psychological Association last month in Washington D.C., that turned out to be a return to the basics: tending to our bodies, connecting in-person, and caring for each other and the most marginalized among us.

In a recent development, joy D. Calloway, president of the Black Women’s Health Imperative, urged attendees to recognize that just because people are functioning at work and home doesn’t mean they’re flourishing. The chronic stress builds up over time and becomes biological harm, Calloway mentioned, citing the weathering theory described by Arline Geronimus, a public health researcher at the University of Michigan. Calloway continued:.

Industry observers note that the field of psychology has an extraordinary opportunity in this moment, not only to measure how people adapt to adversity, but to understand and influence the conditions that create and sustain wellness. . . . Perhaps our greatest blind spot is that we’ve confused resilience with wellness. . . .

According to recent reports, while wellness begins with individuals, it is nurtured by families, strengthened by communities, and made possible by the systems, institutions, and policies that create the conditions for people to thrive. We don’t simply practice wellness; we build it collectively.

Over three days, nearly 8,000 people from 60 different countries attended the conference in person, participating in a program that included 523 different sessions and 1,180 presenters. The scientific poster program included 91 poster sessions, 2,115 posters, and 1,921 presenters.

In sessions on supporting youth mental health, the impact of technology, and “adulthood unmoored,” APA speakers agreed that many of us are struggling to find purpose and optimism amid technological, climate, and global disruption.

Psychologist Ali Mattu noted that over a decade ago, clients sought relief from stress and anxiety, which evolved to seeking relationship and connection support. “Now it’s despair, overwhelm, and meaning,” Mattu told the mainstage audience. “Anyone below the age of 50 here is really searching for meaning, connection, hope, and what do I do with all this overwhelm? What do I do with all of these systems that seem to be collapsing?”.

Perfectionism and the paradox of choice often lie at the root of the overwhelm, said Thomas Curran, associate professor of social psychology at the London School of Economics. “We don’t worry about what we are doing; we worry about what we could be doing,” Curran said. “It’s like swimming in a vast expanse of ocean with nowhere to dock. It’s frightening, and it feels like no matter what we do, it’s never enough.”.

The answer, Curran said: “Microdose bits of discomfort into daily life.”.

According to recent reports, for young people, positive change means pushing back against the ubiquity of technology that purports to connect us but actually keeps us in separate bubbles, staring at our individual feeds. As Nikki Iyer, an undergraduate at the University of California, Berkeley, framed the problem:.

It has been revealed that our generation might be the most connected generation, but we’re also the loneliest generation. We’re the most alienated generation, and we are desperately craving social connection that we don’t know how to tap. . . . There’s so many people around you all the time. You’re on the train together; you’re in parks; you’re in cafes, but everyone is looking down, and that is a horrific way to grow up as social creatures.

It has been revealed that iyer noted that tech firms wouldn’t be spending such unprecedented amounts of money on lobbying and marketing if they didn’t realize there’s a surge of resistance to artificial intelligence and social media dominating our lives. “The world is in our hands if we are willing to make the leap,” she said, noting a return to “weird” hobbies and in-person activity that replace digital time. “I see a lot of young people pushing back against that.”.

AI models were trained on disproportionately white male–oriented data sets, noted Brendesha Tynes, professor of education and psychology at the University of Southern California’s Rossier School of Education, in urging a slowdown in the adoption of AI.

“Anti-Blackness is the default setting in AI,” Tynes mentioned. Young people need skills “to identify, critique, and cope with the algorithmic bias in technologies that they might witness, and then also to eventually create better AI technologies that don’t have anti-Blackness bias.”.

In sessions across the three days of the conference, researchers presented papers and models for identifying and building on resilience in marginalized communities, from LGBTQ+ youth and adults to disabled and racially marginalized people of all ages.

Joshua Parmenter, an assistant professor at Arizona State University, presented a resistance-resilience model with sexual- and gender-diverse people of color, which involves both individually untangling messages that undermine your well-being and finding collective ways to reclaim power. Jules Soper, a researcher at the Oklahoma State University, offered an investigation of resistance strategies that trans and gender-diverse people use in states that are passing anti-trans legislation.

Alvin Thomas, an associate professor at the University of Wisconsin, Madison, noted that anyone can play a positive role in supporting another member of the community. “I have zero kids, and yet I will still call myself a father. I have nephews; I have nieces; I have kids that I mentor from across the Caribbean and across the U.S.,” Thomas said.

Industry observers note that clare M. Mehta, professor of psychology at Emmanuel College and visiting researcher at Royal Holloway, University of London, encouraged everyone to look for ways to be a “villager” who reaches out to another person, and seeks out connection in third spaces. She continued:.

According to recent reports, we have to start going back to the pub again. People have been concerned for years and years that drinking alcohol is bad for your health, but not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health. . . . You don’t have to drink alcohol at the pub. They serve other drinks, right? Go and have a glass of orange juice or like a fizzy water. Not connecting with people socially is even worse for your health.

Young people actually are wired to be a positive force for change, said Eva Telzer, professor of psychology and neuroscience at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill.

According to recent reports, “Young people are superhuman in the way their brains are set up to be risk takers but also to care about others, for peers, and for social interactions to be so crucial,” Telzer said in a question-and-answer period after her mainstage remarks. “That puts them in this perfect place to make change and do good in the world.”.

Industry observers note that even technology has a role to play, Mattu remarked. “AI should be a co-intelligence that enhances the things we are very bad at,” he said, urging people to take the opportunity to define clearly the uniquely human pursuits we should claim, and in which domains technology is appropriate to be a useful aid.

In a recent development, he suggested three criteria for the activities to avoid replacing with AI: what you love, what you have expertise in, and what you hold high standards for. As Jacqueline S. Mattis, a psychologist and dean at Rutgers University, Newark, told her audience:.

We start as this passel of cells, and then we end up laughing, and that’s amazing. You get to experience the magnificence of being able to feel affection for another human being, so much so that you will sacrifice everything for them. That’s amazing. . . . All of that is what defines us as truly human and defines this thing called life as worth living.

Katherine Reynolds Lewis is the special projects editor at the Greater Good Science Center and author of the Good News About Bad Behavior. She is an award-winning science journalist with bylines in the Atlantic, Fortune, New York Times, Undark, and Washington Post.

#138766. Industry News: Scientists discover a hidden messaging system deep inside the brain

📅 23 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1066 w)
